content: Manual therapies, which are based on similar proposed biological mechanisms, are frequently employed in the treatment of asthma. These therapies are administered by a range of practitioners, including physiotherapists, respiratory therapists, chiropractors, and osteopathic physicians. A systematic review that spans these disciplines is necessary to evaluate their effectiveness. The objective of this review was to assess the evidence regarding the effects of manual therapies in treating individuals with bronchial asthma. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across general databases such as EMBASE, CINAHL, and MEDLINE, as well as specialized databases like the Cochrane Complementary Medicine Field, Cochrane Rehabilitation Field, Index to Chiropractic Literature (ICL), and Manual, Alternative and Natural Therapy Index System (MANTIS). Additionally, bibliographies of included studies were reviewed, and authors of known studies were contacted to gather information on both published and unpublished trials. The most recent search was completed in August 2004. The inclusion criteria for trials were as follows: they had to be randomized, involve children or adults diagnosed with asthma, evaluate one or more types of manual therapy, and include clinical outcomes with observation periods of at least two weeks. Data extraction and quality assessment of the trials were independently performed by three reviewers using a standardized form. Out of 473 unique citations, 68 full-text articles were reviewed, and nine citations corresponding to three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 156 patients met the inclusion criteria. Statistical pooling of the trials was not feasible due to differences in patient populations and outcomes across studies, even when similar interventions were examined. Two trials investigated chiropractic spinal manipulation. One of these trials was of good methodological quality, but neither trial demonstrated significant differences between chiropractic manipulation and a sham procedure for any of the measured outcomes. Another small trial compared massage therapy to a relaxation control group and reported significant improvements in several lung function parameters. However, this study had poor reporting standards, and its findings have not been independently confirmed. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support the use of manual therapies for the treatment of asthma. They emphasized the need for adequately powered RCTs that evaluate the effects of manual therapies on clinically meaningful outcomes. Future studies should ensure blinding of outcome assessors, report on the costs of care, and document any adverse events. At present, the evidence is inadequate to either endorse or dismiss the use of manual therapy for asthma management.
